question: In November 2025, the national examination for admission to the tour guide profession took place in Italy. The Ministry of Tourism has presented it as a structural reform of the sector and it has been included in the framework of measures linked to the national recovery plan. Only around 12 000 of the more than 29 000 candidates who applied sat the written exam and only 1.86 % of participants were successful.

This outcome raises major questions and appears disproportionate to the needs of a sector that is of strategic importance for the Italian and European economy and characterised by a chronic shortage of qualified staff, especially in cultural and multilingual tourism.

Issues have also been reported in relation to the excessively superficial nature of the test, which focuses on fact-based learning, thereby excluding highly qualified profiles, and in relation to the lack of clear public data on how the exam was funded and the reporting of costs relating to the exam process, estimated at over EUR 1 million.

These issues raise questions about whether the measure is consistent with the objectives of the national recovery plan, whether it complies with the principles of proportionality and efficiency and whether public resources are being used properly. In light of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Was the initiative funded, even just partially, with national recovery plan resources or EU funds?
Does it consider this admission system and the result achieved to be consistent with European objectives in the areas of employment, skills and the domestic market?
Does it intend to initiate checks into the public resources used?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.5.2026) Italy's Recovery and Resilience plan (RRP)1 includes reform 4.1 on the regulation ordering of the professions of tourist guides, linked to milestone M1C3-10 on the definition of a national standard for tourist guides, which does not cover the organisation of the examination.
The Commission approved the RRP2 and its costing assessment, as per the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) Regulation3.

The Commission positively assessed milestone M1C3-10 in its preliminary assessment of the sixth payment request4, which entailed a minimum national standard for the ordering of the profession of tourist guides5 that fully replaced the former fragmentation and the absence of a nation-wide applicable legislation. The implementing Decree6 provides for the elements considered as the minimum national standard.

The current legislative framework as such is considered to comply with the requirements contained in the Council Implementing Decision7. The reform, within the framework of the RRP, did not provide for associated funding in the form of investment. The Commission raised to Italy that any regulation affecting access to professions must be justified and proportionate under EU law and its impact monitored.
While exams are a national responsibility, the Commission stresses that access to regulated professions should not face disproportionate or unjustified barriers and must comply with EU law.

Concerning employment and skills objectives, the Commission recalls that reforms supported under the RRF are expected to contribute to improving labour market participation and addressing skills shortages, in line with relevant EU law and initiatives8. Beyond the Commission’s role as Treaty guardian, Member States must ensure their laws comply with Union and national law.
